title: General Surgery Diploma — Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology, Lecture 1

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the primary basis of 'Morphological Diagnosis' in diagnostic surgical pathology?
options: Serological antibody titers alone
Macroscopic (gross) and microscopic examination to identify disease patterns, tissue architecture, and cellular morphology
Radiological imaging without tissue sampling
Urine biochemical dipstick analysis
questions.explanation: Morphological diagnosis combines naked-eye gross inspection with microscopic evaluation of architecture and cytomorphology.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 3 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology: • Morphological Diagnosis: Macroscopic & microscopic examination to identify disease patterns, tissue architecture, cellular morphology.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: Which five foundational pillars govern best practice in diagnostic surgical pathology according to the lecture?
options: Tissue Integrity, Chain of Custody, Clinico-Pathological Correlation, Representativeness, and Turnaround Time
Anesthesia depth, suture gauge, antibiotic prophylaxis, blood pressure, and drain output
Cost reduction, rapid discharge, outpatient follow-up, physiotherapy, and diet
Gram staining, blood culture, sensitivity testing, viral PCR, and ELISA
questions.explanation: Accurate pathology requires intact tissue, unbroken chain of custody, correlation with clinical/imaging data, representative sampling, and timely reporting.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slides 3–4 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology: • Five Pillars: Tissue Integrity | Chain of Custody | Clinico-Pathological Correlation | Representativeness | Turnaround Time.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: Why is 'Chain of Custody' legally and clinically critical in surgical pathology?
options: It determines the surgeon's operative fee
It ensures unbroken documentation from excision in theatre to the final pathology report, preventing specimen mix-ups
It speeds up formalin evaporation
It eliminates the need for patient identifiers
questions.explanation: A pathology report is a medicolegal document; tracking every handoff prevents catastrophic patient or site misidentification.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 3 — Chain of Custody: • Chain of Custody: Unbroken documentation from excision to report. Each step is legally and clinically critical.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is a major cause of false-negative or missed diagnoses directly related to biopsy technique?
options: Using 10% neutral buffered formalin
Sampling error (failing to obtain a sample that truly represents the lesion)
Submitting a clinical history on the request form
Labeling the container with two identifiers
questions.explanation: Sampling necrotic centers or adjacent reactive tissue instead of viable diagnostic lesion leads to false-negative pathology reports.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 4 — Representativeness: • Representativeness: The sample must represent the lesion. Sampling error is a major cause of missed diagnoses.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is considered the 'cornerstone of diagnosis' during microscopic analysis of a surgical specimen?
options: Container weight
Tissue architecture, disease pattern, and cellular/nuclear morphology
Fixative color
Surgical glove size
questions.explanation: Evaluation of cellular and nuclear morphology alongside architectural arrangement remains the definitive foundation of histopathology.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — Microscopic Analysis: • Microscopic analysis: Tissue architecture | Disease pattern | Cellular and nuclear morphology (cornerstone of diagnosis).

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the primary diagnostic and predictive role of Immunohistochemistry (IHC) in surgical pathology?
options: Measuring gross specimen dimensions in 3D
Using antibodies to detect specific antigens/proteins to identify tumor origin (diagnostic) and hormone receptor status (predictive)
Sterilizing surgical instruments
Replacing routine H&E fixation
questions.explanation: IHC utilizes antigen-antibody binding to classify poorly differentiated tumors and determine predictive markers like ER/PR/HER2.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — Immunohistochemistry: • Immunohistochemistry: Using antibodies to detect specific antigens and protein → Helping identify origin of tumor (diagnostic) | Predictive: hormone receptors status.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the main clinical purpose of Molecular Studies (analyzing DNA and RNA) on tumor specimens?
options: Assessing macroscopic margin ink
Detecting genetic markers to guide targeted therapy and assess disease prognosis
Preventing crush artefact during forceps handling
Determining the exact time of specimen collection
questions.explanation: Molecular profiling detects actionable mutations (e.g., BRAF, EGFR, KRAS) that direct targeted oncological therapies.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — Molecular Studies: • Molecular studies: Analyzing DNA, RNA to detect genetic markers → Guide target therapy | Assess the prognosis of disease.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the standard routine turnaround time (TAT) for general surgical specimens (routine biopsies and excisions)?
options: 15–30 minutes
2–5 working days
4–6 weeks
24 hours maximum for all cases
questions.explanation: Standard processing, embedding, sectioning, H&E staining, and pathologist review typically take 2 to 5 working days.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Turnaround Time: • Routine surgical specimens (biopsies and excisions): typically, 2–5 working days.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the expected turnaround time for small biopsies versus large or complex surgical resection specimens?
options: Small biopsies: 1–3 working days; Large/complex specimens: 5–10 working days or longer
Small biopsies: 10–14 days; Large specimens: 15 minutes
Both take exactly 6 hours
Large specimens are always reported faster than small biopsies
questions.explanation: Large resections require overnight fixation, extensive grossing, multiple tissue blocks, and decalcification/special stains if needed.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Turnaround Time: • Small biopsies: 1–3 working days | Large or complex specimens: 5–10 working days or longer.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: How long does an intra-operative Frozen Section consultation typically take to report back to the surgeon?
options: 2–5 working days
15–30 minutes
6–8 hours
24 hours
questions.explanation: Frozen section provides rapid intra-operative pathologic feedback within 15–30 minutes while the patient remains under anesthesia.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 & Slide 12 — Frozen Sections: • Frozen sections: intraoperative (15–30 minutes).

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the approximate diagnostic sensitivity of an intra-operative frozen section biopsy?
options: 100% with zero discordance
questions.explanation: Frozen section has ~95% sensitivity, but permanent paraffin sections remain the gold standard and may occasionally revise frozen diagnoses.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 — The Pathologist's Role in Surgical Care: • ~95% Sensitivity of frozen section biopsy | 100% Specimens require proper fixation.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: Which of the following represents the Pathologist's key POST-OPERATIVE responsibilities?
options: Definitive histopathology & staging, prognostic markers (grade, vascular invasion, resection margins), and predictive markers (receptor status, molecular profiling)
Performing pre-operative fine needle aspiration only
Administering general anesthesia
Obtaining informed surgical consent
questions.explanation: Post-operative pathology establishes TNM staging, margin clearance, histological grade, lymphovascular invasion, and biomarker profile.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 — The Pathologist's Role in Surgical Care: • Post-operative: Definitive histopathology & staging | Prognostic markers: Grade, vascular invasion, resection margins | Predictive markers: Receptor status, molecular profiling.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: Which of the following are classified as PROGNOSTIC markers determined by the pathologist?
options: Tumor grade, vascular invasion, and resection margin status
Patient's blood group and Rh factor
Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c
Serum amylase and lipase
questions.explanation: Prognostic markers predict the natural clinical outcome and risk of recurrence independent of specific targeted therapy.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 — Key Responsibilities: • Prognostic markers: Grade, vascular invasion, resection margins.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: Why must pathological findings ALWAYS be interpreted via Clinico-Pathological Correlation?
options: Because pathology slides never show cellular changes
Because morphological findings must be integrated with patient age, anatomical site, clinical history, and radiological imaging to reach an accurate diagnosis
Because pathologists do not have access to microscopes
Because clinical history replaces tissue biopsy
questions.explanation: Identical histological patterns (e.g., granulomatous inflammation or osteoid production) can represent completely different diseases depending on age, site, and imaging.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 3 — Clinico-Pathological Correlation: • Clinico-Pathological Correlation: Pathological findings must always be interpreted in the clinical context — age, site, history, imaging.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: Which step in gross examination depends largely on proper specimen orientation by the surgeon?
options: Ordering special stains
Cutting/sectioning the specimen in the proper anatomical plane to accurately assess surgical margins
Weighing the formalin jar
Printing the patient's barcode
questions.explanation: Without accurate orientation, the pathologist cannot determine which anatomical margin is close or involved by tumor.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 — Gross Examination: • Gross examination: Inspecting the specimen by naked eye | Cut the specimen in proper way (depends largely on good orientation).

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: When a case requires special stains, immunohistochemistry, molecular tests, or expert consultation, what happens to the turnaround time?
options: It decreases to 15 minutes
It requires additional days to weeks beyond routine reporting time
It is cancelled automatically
It stays strictly at 24 hours
questions.explanation: Ancillary testing adds sequential laboratory processing cycles and specialist review time.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 6 — Turnaround Time: • Cases requiring special stain, immune stains, molecular tests or more expert consultation: more additional days to weeks.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What percentage of surgical specimens require proper fixation (or appropriate handling protocol)?
options: Only malignant specimens
questions.explanation: Every single tissue specimen removed during surgery requires strict adherence to fixation or fresh-transport protocols.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 — Key Stat Callout: • 100% Specimens require proper fixation.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.topic: Core Principles, Pathologist's Role & Turnaround Time
questions.stem: What is the medicolegal status of a surgical pathology report?
options: An informal verbal note
A formal legal document in which accuracy is paramount
A temporary billing receipt
Optional documentation
questions.explanation: The pathology report serves as the definitive legal record of diagnosis and guides irreversible surgical or oncological interventions.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 7 — Medicolegal Responsibility: • Medicolegal: Report is a legal document — accuracy is paramount.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What does Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) collect, and what are its classic clinical indications?
options: Large bone cylinders; indicated for osteosarcoma
Samples of cells and fluid using a very small needle; indicated for thyroid nodules, lymph nodes, salivary glands, and superficial soft tissue masses
Full-thickness skin cores; indicated for psoriasis
Whole organ resections; indicated for staging
questions.explanation: FNA is a rapid, minimally invasive outpatient cytological sampling technique ideal for thyroid, salivary, and nodal lesions.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA): • FNA: Medical procedure collects samples of cells and fluid | Very small needle | Indications: Thyroid, lymph nodes, salivary gland, superficial soft tissue.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the major diagnostic limitation of Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) compared to Core Needle Biopsy (CNB)?
options: FNA requires general anesthesia
FNA provides NO tissue architecture and CANNOT distinguish between in-situ and invasive carcinoma
FNA takes 3 weeks to process
FNA cannot be used on thyroid nodules
questions.explanation: Because FNA aspirates disaggregated cells rather than intact tissue strips, stromal invasion cannot be evaluated.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — FNA Limitations: • Limitations of FNA: No tissue architecture; cannot distinguish in-situ vs invasive.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: How should Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) samples be handled immediately after collection?
options: Placed in 10% formalin for 48 hours
Prepared as air-dried or wet-fixed smears (plus a cell block if bloody/fluid-rich)
Frozen in liquid nitrogen
Placed in glutaraldehyde only
questions.explanation: Air-dried smears are stained with Giemsa/Diff-Quik while alcohol wet-fixed smears are stained with Papanicolaou stain.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — FNA Handling: • Handling of FNA: Air-dried or wet-fixed smears; cell block if bloody.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What tissue does a Core Needle Biopsy (CNB) obtain, and what are its main advantages over FNA?
options: Cells and fluid only; faster than FNA
Small cylinders of intact tissue using a hollow needle; preserves tissue architecture and allows receptor and molecular studies
Superficial epidermal shavings; no bleeding risk
Whole lymph nodes; requires general anesthesia
questions.explanation: CNB preserves stromal relationships, enabling differentiation of in-situ vs. invasive cancer and providing ample tissue for IHC/biomarkers.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — Core Needle Biopsy (CNB): • CNB: Removes small cylinders of tissue using hollow needle | Advantages: Tissue architecture preserved; receptor & molecular studies.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the classic organ indications and potential complications/limitations of Core Needle Biopsy (CNB)?
options: Indications: Breast, prostate, liver, kidney, lung, bone; Limitations: Sampling error and hematoma risk
Indications: Cornea and retina; Limitations: Cataract
Indications: Epidermal warts only; Limitations: Keloid
Indications: Cerebrospinal fluid; Limitations: Meningitis
questions.explanation: CNB is the standard pre-operative biopsy for breast, prostate, liver, and renal masses, requiring immediate 10% NBF fixation.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 9 — CNB Indications & Limitations: • Indications: Breast, prostate, liver, kidney, lung, bone | Limitations: Sampling error; haematoma risk | Handling: Place immediately in 10% NBF.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is an Incisional Biopsy, and what is its clinical goal?
options: Complete removal of a small lesion; both diagnostic and curative
Partial removal of a lesion; goal is diagnosis ONLY (NOT curative)
Superficial horizontal shave of the epidermis
Needle aspiration of cyst fluid
questions.explanation: Incisional biopsy is reserved for large tumors or mucosal/soft-tissue masses where complete excision requires definitive pre-operative histological diagnosis.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 10 — Incisional Biopsy: • Incisional Biopsy: Definition: Partial removal of lesion | Goal: Diagnosis only - NOT curative | Indications: Large lesions, bone & soft tissue tumours, mucosal lesions.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the golden technical rule when performing an Incisional Biopsy regarding tissue selection?
options: Sample exclusively from the central necrotic core
Include the interface of normal and abnormal tissue, and AVOID central necrotic areas (submit viable peripheral tissue)
Crush the tissue with toothed forceps before fixation
Mix samples from multiple sites into a single formalin pot
questions.explanation: Central tumor necrosis yields non-diagnostic debris; the viable periphery and normal-tumor transition zone show active invasion.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 10 — Incisional Biopsy Key Rules: • Key rule: Include interface of normal & abnormal tissue | Avoid: Central necrotic areas -> submit viable peripheral tissue | Send separately if >1 site sampled.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is an Excisional Biopsy, and how should the surgeon handle the specimen before sending it to the lab?
options: Partial removal; cut it into multiple slices in theatre
Complete removal of the entire lesion (both diagnostic and therapeutic); DO NOT section before sending to the lab, and document orientation with sutures
Superficial shave biopsy; leave on a dry tray for 2 hours
Needle aspiration; place in normal saline
questions.explanation: Never bivalve or slice an excisional specimen in the OR, as this destroys margin integrity and prevents accurate inking by the pathologist.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 10 — Excisional Biopsy: • Excisional Biopsy: Complete removal of lesion — diagnostic & therapeutic | Do NOT section before sending to lab | Document orientation with sutures (short = superior, long = lateral).

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the classic clinical indications for an Excisional Biopsy?
options: Massive retroperitoneal sarcomas
Small skin lesions, enlarged lymph nodes, and small soft tissue masses
Diffuse interstitial lung disease
Metastatic liver lesions
questions.explanation: When a lesion is small enough to be completely removed with clear margins safely, excisional biopsy achieves both diagnosis and cure.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 10 — Excisional Biopsy Indications: • Indications for Excisional Biopsy: Small skin lesions, lymph nodes, small soft tissue masses.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is a Punch Biopsy, and what are its primary dermatological indications?
options: A superficial horizontal slice; used for seborrheic keratosis
A cylindrical full-thickness skin sample (2–8 mm); indicated for inflammatory dermatoses and melanocytic lesions
A hollow needle biopsy of the liver
An intra-operative frozen tissue block
questions.explanation: A 2–8 mm circular punch blade obtains epidermis, dermis, and subcutis in a single full-thickness cylinder.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 11 — Punch Biopsy: • Punch Biopsy: Cylindrical full-thickness skin sample (2–8 mm) | Indications: Inflammatory dermatoses, melanocytic lesions | Submit in formalin; note exact site.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Why must a Shave Biopsy NEVER be used for a suspected malignant melanoma?
options: Because it requires general anesthesia
Because a shave biopsy cuts horizontally through the superficial dermis and CANNOT assess deep margins or Breslow tumor thickness
Because formalin dissolves melanocytes
Because it causes excessive bone bleeding
questions.explanation: Melanoma staging and prognosis depend critically on Breslow depth of vertical invasion; transecting the base via shave biopsy ruins staging.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 11 — Shave Biopsy Limitation: • Shave Biopsy: Horizontal cut through superficial dermis | Indications: Raised skin lesions, seborrhoeic keratosis | Limitation: Does not assess deep margins -> do NOT use for suspected melanoma.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the three primary intra-operative indications for a Frozen Section (FS) biopsy?
options: Margin assessment, lymph node status (e.g., sentinel node), and distinguishing benign vs. malignant lesions intra-operatively
Routine diagnosis of fatty lipomas, bone tumors, and dry necrotic eschars
Electron microscopy, microbiology culture, and flow cytometry
Measuring serum tumor markers
questions.explanation: Frozen section is only indicated when the immediate intra-operative result will directly alter the surgical procedure being performed.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Frozen Section (FS): • Frozen Section: Intra-operative rapid diagnosis (~15–30 min) | Indications: Margin assessment, lymph node status, distinguish benign vs malignant.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: How MUST a tissue specimen for Frozen Section be transported to the pathology laboratory?
options: Immersed in 10% neutral buffered formalin
NEVER fix in formalin — send FRESH, immediately on ice or dry, with prior notification to the lab
Placed in 70% ethanol overnight
Fixed in glutaraldehyde
questions.explanation: Formalin fixes tissue proteins and prevents freezing in the cryostat; frozen section specimens must arrive fresh and unfixed.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Frozen Section Handling: • NEVER fix in formalin -> send fresh, immediately on ice or dry | Communication: Surgeon must notify lab in advance.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which tissue types are major technical limitations/contraindications for Frozen Section examination?
options: Lymph nodes and breast margins
Bone (calcified tissue) and fat (adipose tissue), plus freezing artefacts
Thyroid nodules and mucosal margins
Smooth muscle and fibrous tissue
questions.explanation: Bone cannot be cut on a cryostat blade without decalcification, and fat fails to freeze solidly at standard cryostat temperatures (-20°C).
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Frozen Section Limitations: • Limitations of Frozen Section: Artefact, bone, fat | Discordance: Frozen diagnosis may be revised on permanent sections.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Why is advance communication between the surgeon and pathologist essential before sending a Frozen Section?
options: So the cryostat can be cooled and prepared, and the pathologist understands the exact clinical question
To obtain insurance pre-authorization
To prepare formalin jars
To schedule outpatient follow-up
questions.explanation: Alerting the pathology team ensures immediate cryostat readiness and minimizes anesthesia duration.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 12 — Frozen Section Communication: • Communication: Surgeon must notify lab in advance.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: If a lymph node biopsy is suspected to be a lymphoma requiring Flow Cytometry, how must the specimen be submitted?
options: Fixed in 10% NBF for 24 hours
Must be sent FRESH (unfixed) immediately to the laboratory
Fixed in glutaraldehyde
Air-dried on a glass slide
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry requires viable, intact cell suspensions to immunophenotype surface markers; formalin fixation cross-links proteins and kills cells.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Fresh vs. Fixed Specimens Table: • Flow cytometry / lymphoma: Fresh Specimen = Must be fresh | Fixed Specimen (10% NBF) = X Not possible.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: If a surgical specimen requires Microbiology Culture (e.g., suspected tuberculous lymphadenitis or abscess), how must it be submitted?
options: In 10% neutral buffered formalin
Must be sent FRESH in a sterile container without fixative
In Bouin's solution
Wrapped in dry non-sterile gauze
questions.explanation: Formalin is bactericidal and destroys microorganisms, rendering culture impossible.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Fresh vs. Fixed Specimens Table: • Microbiology culture: Fresh Specimen = Must be fresh, sterile | Fixed Specimen (10% NBF) = X Not possible.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which fixative is specifically required if a specimen is intended for Electron Microscopy (EM)?
options: 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin
Glutaraldehyde (NOT 10% NBF)
Normal saline (0.9% NaCl)
Tap water
questions.explanation: Glutaraldehyde preserves ultrastructural organelle membranes for transmission electron microscopy far better than routine formalin.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Fresh vs. Fixed Specimens Table: • Electron microscopy: Fix in glutaraldehyde (not NBF) | Fixed Specimen (10% NBF) = X Not suitable.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Can molecular studies (DNA/RNA mutation analysis) be performed on routine Formalin-Fixed Paraffin-Embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks?
options: No, molecular studies are strictly impossible on FFPE blocks
Yes — while fresh tissue is optimal, FFPE blocks are adequate for routine molecular studies
Only if fixed in normal saline
Only if frozen in liquid nitrogen
questions.explanation: Modern PCR and Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) protocols routinely extract DNA/RNA from well-fixed FFPE blocks.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Fresh vs. Fixed Specimens Table: • Molecular studies: Fresh Specimen = Optimal | Fixed Specimen (10% NBF) = FFPE blocks adequate.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: When multiple sites are sampled during an incisional biopsy procedure, how must they be submitted?
options: All combined in one large container to save space
Submitted in separate, individually labeled containers specifying each exact anatomical site
Wrapped together in a single gauze sponge
Placed in saline without labels
questions.explanation: Mixing multiple biopsies in one jar makes it impossible to know which anatomical site harbors malignancy.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 10 & Slide 14 — Specimen Submission Rules: • Send separately if >1 site sampled | DO NOT mix multiple specimens in one container.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the correct 5-step sequence for handling surgical specimens in the operating theatre?
options: 1. Remove Cleanly → 2. Orient & Ink → 3. Measure → 4. Fix Promptly → 5. Label Correctly
1. Cut into pieces → 2. Leave on dry tray → 3. Put in saline → 4. Label lid → 5. Send next week
1. Fix in formalin → 2. Send for frozen section → 3. Crush with forceps → 4. Wash ink off
1. Label lid → 2. Place in plastic bag without pot → 3. Add tap water
questions.explanation: Following this exact workflow preserves tissue morphology, margin orientation, and patient identity.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 13 — Handling of Surgical Specimens (5 Steps): • 1. Remove Cleanly (avoid crush artefact) → 2. Orient & Ink (mark margins before bivalving) → 3. Measure (3D dimensions) → 4. Fix Promptly (10% NBF, 10:1 ratio) → 5. Label Correctly.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the standard fixative of choice for routine histopathological examination?
options: 0.9% Normal saline
10% Neutral Buffered Formalin (NBF)
5% Dextrose in water
Hydrogen peroxide
questions.explanation: 10% NBF (4% formaldehyde buffered to neutral pH) prevents autolysis and preserves cellular architecture and antigenicity.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Fixation Key Facts: • Fixative of choice: 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin (NBF) | DO NOT use saline instead of formalin for routine histology.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the required minimum volume ratio of fixative (10% NBF) to tissue specimen?
options: 1:1 (equal volume)
10:1 (10 parts fixative to 1 part tissue)
1:10 (1 part fixative to 10 parts tissue)
questions.explanation: An adequate 10:1 volume ratio prevents dilution of formaldehyde by tissue fluids and ensures complete penetration.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Fixation Key Facts: • Ratio: 10 parts fixative : 1 part tissue.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the approximate tissue penetration rate of 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin?
options: ~10 mm/hour
~1 mm/hour
~1 cm/minute
~0.01 mm/day
questions.explanation: Because formalin penetrates slowly (~1 mm/hr), large solid organs must be sliced (after inking) to allow fixative access to deep tumors.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Fixation Key Facts: • Penetration rate: ~1 mm/hour | Minimum fixation: 6–8 hours; optimal 24 hours.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the minimum fixation time and the optimal fixation time in 10% NBF for routine surgical specimens?
options: Minimum: 15 minutes; Optimal: 1 hour
Minimum: 6–8 hours; Optimal: 24 hours
Minimum: 7 days; Optimal: 30 days
Minimum: 30 seconds; Optimal: 5 minutes
questions.explanation: Under-fixation (<6 hours) leads to poor nuclear detail and unreliable immunohistochemistry, whereas 24 hours provides ideal cross-linking.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Fixation Key Facts: • Minimum fixation: 6–8 hours; optimal 24 hours.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: For optimal Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and breast hormone receptor (ER/PR/HER2) assessment, within what timeframe post-excision should tissue ideally be placed in 10% NBF?
options: Within ≤ 1 hour post-excision (cold ischemia time < 1 hour)
After 12 hours on the surgical bench
After 48 hours in saline
Timing does not affect receptor status
questions.explanation: Prolonged cold ischemia (>1 hour) degrades labile receptor proteins (especially ER/PR/HER2), causing false-negative predictive biomarker results.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Fresh vs. Fixed Specimens Table: • IHC / receptor status: Best if fixed ≤ 1h post-excision | Transport time > 30 min -> Risk of autolysis if unfixed.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What happens if a fresh, unfixed surgical specimen experiences a transport delay of > 30 minutes without refrigeration or fixation?
options: Enhanced nuclear staining
Risk of tissue autolysis (enzymatic self-digestion) and drying artefact
Spontaneous sterilization
Improved frozen section clarity
questions.explanation: Delayed immersion in formalin initiates lysosomal autolysis and bacterial overgrowth, permanently ruining cellular morphology.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 — Transport Time > 30 min: • Transport time > 30 min: Fresh specimen = Risk of autolysis | Fixed specimen (10% NBF) = Safe for routine studies.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which of the following is strictly listed under 'DO NOT' rules during surgical specimen handling?
options: DO NOT cut or section the specimen before inking; DO NOT allow drying; DO NOT use saline instead of formalin; DO NOT mix multiple specimens in one container
DO NOT label the container body
DO NOT measure the specimen
DO NOT send a request form
questions.explanation: Placing tissue in normal saline instead of formalin allows ongoing autolysis because saline is not a fixative.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Fixation DO NOT List: • DO NOT: Cut or section the specimen before inking | Allow drying -> immediately immerse in fixative | Use saline instead of formalin | Mix multiple specimens in one container.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is a 'Tissue Artefact' in diagnostic pathology?
options: A normal anatomical variant
An artificial distortion of tissue induced during the biopsy procedure, surgical handling, or laboratory processing
A benign mesenchymal neoplasm
A calibrated microscope lens
questions.explanation: Artefacts mimic or obscure true pathology (e.g., crush artefact mimicking small cell carcinoma) and can render a biopsy uninterpretable.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 16 — Tissue Artefacts: • Artefact: Artificial distortion of tissue that are induced during biopsy procedure, handling and processing.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What causes 'Crush Artefact', and how does it affect microscopic diagnosis?
options: Leaving tissue in formalin for 24 hours
Squeezing or grasping delicate tissue tightly with forceps or clamps, causing severe nuclear smearing and artificial distortion
Using waterproof ink on the container
Placing a short suture at the superior pole
questions.explanation: Forceps crush shears fragile nuclei (especially in small biopsies and lymphoid/neuroendocrine tumors), obscuring cellular detail.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 16 — Crush Artefact: • Crush artefact: Artificial distortion of tissue | Caused by squeezing by forceps.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What causes 'Drying Artefact', and what is its histological consequence?
options: Immersion in 10% NBF
Leaving tissue exposed on a dry surgical tray or dry gauze, causing severe cellular shrinkage and distortion
Immediate transport on ice
Using a 10:1 formalin ratio
questions.explanation: Evaporation of cellular water causes pyknotic, hyperchromatic, distorted cells that cannot be reliably evaluated.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 16 — Drying Artefact: • Drying artefact: Leaving tissue on dry surgical tray | Causes severe cellular distortion.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the histological consequences of 'Fixation Artefact' (delayed or inadequate fixation)?
options: Improved antigen retrieval
Cell swelling, shrinkage, and poor staining quality
Enhanced mitotic figure clarity
Zero impact on H&E slides
questions.explanation: Inadequate fixation causes uneven dye uptake and structural collapse during paraffin processing.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 16 — Fixation Artefact: • Fixation artefact: Delayed or inadequate fixation | Cause cell swelling, shrinkage and poor staining.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Why does anatomical orientation of a surgical excision specimen matter clinically?
options: It determines the patient's hospital room number
Accurate margin assessment depends on knowing which specimen surface corresponds to which anatomical direction; without orientation, a positive margin cannot be re-excised precisely
It prevents formalin leakage
It speeds up immunohistochemistry
questions.explanation: If the deep or medial margin is positive on pathology, proper orientation allows targeted re-excision rather than blind radical re-operation.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 19 — Orientation of Surgical Specimens: • Why Orientation Matters: Accurate margin assessment depends on knowing which surface corresponds to which anatomical direction. Without orientation, a positive margin cannot be re-excised precisely.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the standard Suture Orientation Convention described in the lecture?
options: Short suture = Superior; Long suture = Lateral (or as agreed with the pathology lab)
Short suture = Deep; Long suture = Skin
Two knots = Benign; Three knots = Malignant
Silk suture = Left; Vicryl = Right
questions.explanation: Two orthogonal sutures (e.g., short superior, long lateral) uniquely define all six anatomical faces (superior, inferior, medial, lateral, anterior, posterior) in 3D space.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 19 — Suture Convention: • Suture Convention: Short suture = Superior | Long suture = Lateral (or as agreed with lab).

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the standard Multi-Color Ink Convention used to mark surgical specimen margins?
options: Black = Posterior; Blue = Anterior; Yellow = Superior; Green = Inferior
Red = Normal; White = Tumor
All margins painted with water-soluble pen
Ink is applied only after paraffin embedding
questions.explanation: Differential colored inks remain visible under the microscope, allowing exact identification of which margin is closest to tumor cells.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 19 — Ink Convention: • Ink Convention: Different colour inks for different margins: Black = posterior | Blue = anterior | Yellow = superior | Green = inferior.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the purpose of placing a 'Radial suture' or metal clip on an excision specimen?
options: To close the skin incision
To mark specific areas of clinical concern or the closest margin for targeted re-excision guidance
To weigh the specimen
To neutralize formalin
questions.explanation: Highlighting a suspicious focal area alerts the pathologist to take extra sections from that exact spot.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 19 — Additional Marking: • Additional Marking: Radial suture / clip: Used to mark areas of concern or closest margin for re-excision guidance.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the four 'Golden Rules for Orientation' of surgical specimens?
options: 1. Agree on a suture convention with pathology and apply consistently; 2. Attach orientation note & communicate verbally; 3. Never re-orient after excision (orient in situ if possible); 4. Document orientation diagram in operative note
1. Cut specimen first; 2. Guess orientation after fixation; 3. Label lid only; 4. Use non-waterproof ink
1. Place in saline; 2. Freeze before inking; 3. Omit clinical history; 4. Send next month
1. Use one jar for all tumors; 2. Never draw diagrams; 3. Ignore close margins; 4. Skip sutures
questions.explanation: Once an irregular soft-tissue or breast specimen is removed from the body, it loses its anatomical landmarks and cannot be reliably oriented retrospectively.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 20 — Golden Rules for Orientation: • 1. Agree on convention & apply consistently | 2. Attach orientation note & communicate complexity | 3. Never re-orient after excision (orient in situ) | 4. Document diagram in operative note.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Why should orientation sutures ideally be placed while the specimen is still IN SITU (before complete detachment)?
options: Because once excised, symmetrical or fatty specimens rotate and lose their anatomical landmarks, making post-excision re-orientation prone to error
Because sutures cannot penetrate excised tissue
Because formalin dissolves sutures placed outside the body
To prevent bleeding
questions.explanation: Placing the superior and lateral sutures prior to final detachment guarantees 100% anatomical accuracy.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 20 — Golden Rule #3: • 3. Never re-orient after excision — establish orientation while the specimen is still in situ if possible.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Why must a specimen NEVER be bisected/bivalved by the surgeon before margin inking?
options: Because bivalving distorts the true surgical margin, causes the capsule/fat to retract, and allows ink to seep into the cut tumor surface (creating false-positive margins)
Because scalpels cannot cut fresh tissue
Because it doubles the laboratory cost
Because formalin cannot penetrate cut surfaces
questions.explanation: If ink runs into an intra-operative cut, the pathologist will falsely interpret the cut interior as a positive surgical resection margin.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 13 & Slide 14 — Orient & Ink Before Bivalving: • Orient & Ink: Mark margins before bivalving (sutures/ink) | DO NOT cut or section the specimen before inking.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What should be done immediately after removing a clean, intact biopsy specimen in theatre?
options: Leave it on a warm surgical lamp to dry
Orient, measure, and immerse it promptly in 10% NBF (unless fresh tissue is needed for frozen section, flow cytometry, or culture)
Wash it vigorously with tap water for 20 minutes
Squeeze it with hemostats to remove blood
questions.explanation: Prompt fixation halts autolysis within seconds of excision.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 13 & Slide 14 — Immediate Fixation: • Fix Promptly: 10% NBF; ratio 10:1 fixative to tissue | Allow drying -> immediately immerse in fixative.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which surgical specimen requires a documented orientation diagram inside the operative note for medicolegal purposes?
options: Oriented oncological excisions (e.g., wide local excision of breast or skin cancer)
Blood smear slides
Urine cytology
Routine blood cultures
questions.explanation: Recording the exact suture key in the operative note ensures permanent traceability if future re-excision or litigation occurs.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 20 — Golden Rule #4: • 4. Document orientation diagram in the operative note for medicolegal purposes.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What happens if an unfixed specimen is sent in a dry container taking > 30 minutes to reach the lab?
options: Autolysis and drying artefact degrade cellular morphology
Tissue becomes better preserved
Frozen section sensitivity increases to 100%
It acts like glutaraldehyde
questions.explanation: Rapid transport (<30 min) or immediate 10% NBF immersion is mandatory to preserve tissue integrity.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 15 & Slide 16 — Transport Delay & Drying: • Transport time > 30 min -> Risk of autolysis | Leaving tissue on dry surgical tray -> Drying artefact.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which fixative is explicitly contraindicated for routine H&E histology because it causes severe autolysis?
options: 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin
Normal saline (0.9% NaCl)
Buffered formaldehyde
Alcohol-based cytology fixative (for smears)
questions.explanation: Normal saline has zero fixative properties; tissues left in saline rot and autolyze.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 14 — Fixation DO NOT Rule: • DO NOT: Use saline instead of formalin for routine histology.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: How does the pathologist examine the external surface and cut surfaces during Gross Examination?
options: By naked eye inspection, measuring 3D dimensions, describing macroscopic appearance, and sectioning according to orientation
Using an electron microscope only
By culturing the formalin fluid
Without opening the container
questions.explanation: Thorough grossing selects the most representative blocks (tumor, margins, lymph nodes) for microscopic embedding.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 5 & Slide 13 — Gross Examination: • Gross examination: Inspecting the specimen by naked eye | Measure 3D dimensions; describe macroscopic appearance | Cut in proper way.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Where MUST the patient identification label be placed on a surgical specimen container?
options: On the removable lid ONLY
Directly on the body/side of the container itself — NEVER on the lid
On the outside of the transport bag only
Nowhere, as the request form is sufficient
questions.explanation: Lids are routinely removed and swapped during grossing in the pathology lab; a label on the lid can easily end up on the wrong patient's jar.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 18 — Best Practice Labeling: • Write on the container NOT the lid | Common Errors: Lid labelled not the container.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: How many unique patient identifiers are mandatory on every surgical specimen label?
options: At least ONE (e.g., first name only)
At least TWO patient identifiers (e.g., Patient full name as per ID with no abbreviations + Date of birth / Hospital ID)
Zero identifiers if the surgeon signs the form
Only the bed number
questions.explanation: Using at least two unique identifiers (full name + DOB/hospital MRN) eliminates misidentification between patients with similar names.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 17 & Slide 18 — Mandatory Label Information: • Patient full name (as per ID, no abbreviations) + Date of birth / Hospital ID -> Two identifiers required.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which eight items constitute the MANDATORY information on a surgical specimen container label?
options: 1. Patient full name; 2. DOB/Hospital ID; 3. Date & time of collection; 4. Anatomical site & laterality; 5. Nature of specimen; 6. Surgeon's name; 7. Fixative used; 8. Orientation markers
1. Ward color; 2. Nurse shift; 3. Blood pressure; 4. Pulse; 5. Temperature; 6. Weight; 7. Height; 8. BMI
1. Hospital address; 2. Billing code; 3. Insurance ID; 4. Room number; 5. Bed number; 6. Diet; 7. Allergies; 8. Religion
Only the date and surgeon's initials
questions.explanation: Every single one of these 8 fields is required on the pot label to guarantee safe, traceable pathology processing.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 17 — MANDATORY Label Information Table: • Full name | DOB/Hospital ID | Date & time of collection | Anatomical site & laterality | Nature of specimen | Surgeon's name | Fixative used | Orientation markers.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Why is recording the exact 'Date & Time of Collection' on the specimen label clinically critical?
options: To calculate the surgeon's overtime pay
It is critical for tracking fixation timing (cold ischemia time and minimum 6–8 hr fixation window)
To determine the patient's discharge date
To schedule cleaning of the operating theatre
questions.explanation: Knowing when the specimen was placed in formalin ensures adequate fixation duration before processing and validates receptor testing.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 17 — Mandatory Label Information: • Date & time of collection: Critical for fixation timing.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: When should the specimen container be labeled relative to placing the tissue inside?
options: Before filling with fixative / immediately upon collection, using a waterproof pen or printed barcode label
Two days later when the report is typed
Using a water-soluble pencil that washes off in formalin
Only after the pathologist asks for it
questions.explanation: Alcohol and formalin rapidly dissolve ordinary ballpoint or marker ink, leaving blank unidentifiable containers.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 18 — Best Practice Labeling: • Label before filling with fixative | Waterproof pen or printed labels only | Common Error: Ink that washes off in formalin.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What happens if an UNLABELED surgical specimen arrives at the pathology department?
options: The pathologist guesses the patient's name
The specimen is REJECTED (cannot be processed safely), potentially requiring a repeat invasive procedure and causing severe patient harm
It is automatically reported as benign
It is discarded without notifying the surgeon
questions.explanation: Processing an unlabeled specimen risks issuing a cancer diagnosis to the wrong patient; strict laboratory safety mandates rejection/quarantine.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Consequences of Poor Requests & Common Errors: • Error: Specimen not labelled -> Potential Consequence: Specimen rejected; repeat procedure required; patient harm.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the six main sections (A–F) of a complete Pathology Request Form?
options: A. Patient Demographics; B. Clinical Information; C. Specimen Details; D. Investigations Required; E. Surgeon's Details; F. Special Instructions
A. Anesthesia chart; B. Nursing notes; C. Fluid balance; D. Pharmacy bill; E. Diet sheet; F. Discharge summary
Only Patient Name and Signature
Only Specimen Weight and Fixative Volume
questions.explanation: A complete request form bridges the clinical gap between surgeon and pathologist.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slides 21–22 — The Pathology Request Form (A–F): • A. Patient Demographics | B. Clinical Information | C. Specimen Details | D. Investigations Required | E. Surgeon's Details | F. Special Instructions.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which details must be included under Section B (Clinical Information) of the Pathology Request Form?
options: Relevant clinical history, duration, growth rate, previous treatment (e.g., neoadjuvant chemotherapy/radiotherapy), and relevant imaging findings (US, CT, MRI)
Only the patient's telephone number
Only the suture brand used
The operating room temperature
questions.explanation: Prior radiation or chemotherapy induces bizarre cellular atypia that can mimic malignancy unless the pathologist is informed.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 21 — Section B: Clinical Information: • B. Clinical Information: Relevant history | Duration, growth rate, previous treatment | Relevant imaging findings (ultrasound, CT, MRI).

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the consequence of omitting clinical history on the Pathology Request Form?
options: Faster reporting
Non-specific reporting and failure to consider important differential diagnoses
Automatic molecular profiling
Improved H&E staining
questions.explanation: Clinical context transforms a descriptive histological observation into an actionable specific diagnosis.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Consequences of Poor Requests Table: • Error: Missing clinical history -> Potential Consequence: Non-specific reporting; important differential diagnoses not considered.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the consequence of writing the 'Wrong site or no laterality' (e.g., omitting Left vs. Right breast) on the label or request form?
options: Minor delay with no clinical impact
Specimens mixed up, re-excision performed at the wrong anatomical site, and severe medicolegal consequences
Automatic correction by the computer
Better margin assessment
questions.explanation: Never-event surgical errors (operating on the wrong side) frequently trace back to omitted or inaccurate laterality on pathology forms.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Consequences of Poor Requests Table: • Error: Wrong site or no laterality -> Potential Consequence: Specimens mixed up; re-excision at wrong site; medicolegal consequences.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the potential consequence of failing to state 'Priority' (Urgent vs. Routine) on a Pathology Request Form?
options: Urgent cancer diagnoses are processed as routine, delaying definitive oncological treatment
All specimens are automatically treated as frozen sections
The specimen is rejected
Formalin fixation is skipped
questions.explanation: Flagging urgent/cancer-suspect cases prioritizes rapid tissue processing and expedited pathologist sign-out.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Consequences of Poor Requests Table: • Error: No priority stated -> Potential Consequence: Urgent cancer diagnoses processed as routine; delays treatment.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the consequence of 'Illegible handwriting' on a Pathology Request Form?
options: Transcription errors, reporting delays, and risk of assigning a report to the wrong patient
Improved diagnostic accuracy
Faster immunohistochemical staining
None, as handwritten forms are not read
questions.explanation: Printed electronic orders or clear block capital letters prevent misreading of patient names, sites, and clinical notes.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Consequences of Poor Requests Table: • Error: Illegible handwriting -> Potential Consequence: Transcription error; delays; wrong patient report.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which biohazard and reference information should be included under Section F (Special Instructions) of the Pathology Request Form?
options: Orientation/suture convention used, clinical suspicion (benign/malignant), relevant serology/genetics, HIV/Hepatitis/biohazard status, and previous pathology reference numbers
Patient's favorite meal and room preference
Blood transfusion crossmatch unit numbers only
Post-operative physiotherapy exercises
questions.explanation: Alerting laboratory staff to high-risk infectious specimens (HIV, HBV, HCV, TB) protects personnel during fresh specimen grossing.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 22 — Section F: Special Instructions: • F. Special Instructions: Orientation/suture convention | Clinical suspicion | Relevant serology/genetics | HIV/Hepatitis/biohazard status | Previous pathology reference numbers.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What are the two mandatory requirements for safe SPECIMEN TRANSPORTATION to the pathology laboratory?
options: 1. Secure, leak-proof lid; 2. Proper biohazard precaution (secondary biohazard bag/carrier)
1. Open container lid; 2. Transport in surgeon's pocket
1. Plastic bag without any rigid container; 2. Delayed overnight storage at room temperature
1. Wrapping in dry paper towels; 2. Leaving at reception desk
questions.explanation: Formalin is toxic/carcinogenic and fresh tissues carry infectious risk; rigid containers with tight lids inside sealed biohazard bags are mandatory.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 24 — Specimen Transportation: • Requirements: 1. Secure lid | 2. Proper biohazard precaution.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which three practices MUST be avoided during Specimen Transportation?
options: 1. Unlabeled containers; 2. Delayed submission; 3. Plastic bags without rigid containers
1. Using rigid leak-proof jars; 2. Prompt delivery; 3. Biohazard labeling
1. Sending completed request forms; 2. Using 10% NBF; 3. Two patient identifiers
1. Communicating with the pathologist; 2. Inking margins; 3. Measuring 3D size
questions.explanation: Placing soft tissue directly into a plastic bag without a rigid container causes severe mechanical crush distortion and leakage.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 24 — Specimen Transportation (What to Avoid): • What to avoid: 1. Unlabeled containers | 2. Delayed submission | 3. Plastic bags without containers.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: What is the consequence of providing 'Inadequate fixation details' on the Pathology Request Form?
options: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and molecular tests may fail or yield invalid results
Gross measurement becomes impossible
The patient's hospital ID changes
Frozen section sensitivity increases
questions.explanation: Different fixatives (e.g., Bouin's or alcohol vs. 10% NBF) alter antigen retrieval protocols and nucleic acid integrity.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 23 — Consequences of Poor Requests Table: • Error: Inadequate fixation details -> Potential Consequence: IHC / molecular tests may fail.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: Which details must the surgeon provide under Section E (Surgeon's Details) of the request form?
options: Full name, signature, date & time of operation, priority (urgent/routine), and direct contact details for results discussion
Medical school graduation year only
Home address of the patient
List of all scrub nurses
questions.explanation: Direct contact information allows the pathologist to immediately phone the surgeon regarding unexpected malignancy or critical margin findings.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 22 — Section E: Surgeon's Details: • E. Surgeon's Details: Full name | Signature | Date & time of operation | Priority (urgent / routine) | Contact for results discussion.

questions.subject: PATH1
questions.stem: According to the lecture's final summary, what is the golden rule regarding biopsy selection and communication with the pathologist?
options: Choose biopsy type based on size, site, and suspected diagnosis (no one-size-fits-all approach), and communicate directly with the pathologist to prevent delays and ensure appropriate testing
Always perform a shave biopsy for every skin lesion and avoid calling the lab
Always put every specimen in normal saline first
Slice all tumors in half before sending them to pathology
questions.explanation: Tailoring the biopsy modality to the clinical lesion and maintaining direct surgeon-pathologist communication maximizes diagnostic accuracy and patient safety.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.reference_snapshot: Slide 25 — Key Points Summary: • 1. Choose biopsy type based on size, site and suspected diagnosis — no one-size-fits-all approach | 6. Communicate with your pathologist — a phone call prevents delays and ensures the right tests are ordered.
